i0: We use ***must*** and ***have to*** to say that something is **necessary**: *I **have to** get up early tomorrow. You **must** wear a helmet.*
i1: Their negatives are very different: *You **mustn't** smoke here* (it's not allowed) but *You **don't have to** come* (it isn't necessary). For advice, see [Should and Ought To](/blog/grammar/should-ought-to/).
mht-have-to.s: **have to / has to + base verb** = it's necessary: *I **have to** work on Saturday. She **has to** wear a uniform.*
mht-have-to.b0.h: | I / you / we / they | he / she / it
mht-have-to.b1: *Have to* works like a normal verb: it uses *do / does* for questions and negatives: ***Do** you **have to** work tomorrow?*
mht-have-to.b2: It is very common for rules, routines and things that other people decide: *In my job I **have to** answer a lot of emails.*
mht-have-to.b3: Pronunciation: in fast speech, *have to* sounds like /ˈhæftə/ and *has to* like /ˈhæstə/.
mht-must.t: Must: strong obligation and strong advice
mht-must.s: **must + base verb** for strong obligation, often the speaker's own feeling, and for rules: *I **must** call my mum. You **must** wear a seat belt.*
mht-must.b0: ***Must*** is the same for every person and has no *to*: *I **must** go, she **must** go.* Not *She musts go* or *I must to go*.
mht-must.b2.0: things **we** feel are necessary: *I **must** remember to call Lisa.*
mht-must.b2.1: **rules** and **signs**, often in writing: *Passengers **must** wear a seat belt.*
mht-must.b2.2: strong **recommendations**: *You **must** try this cake. It's amazing!*
mht-must.b3: *Must* is only used for the present and future. For the past, use *had to*: *Yesterday I **had to** work late.* Not *I musted*. See [Must or have to?](#mht-must-vs-have-to)
mht-mustnt-dont-have-to.s: **mustn't** = it's not allowed / don't do it. **don't have to** = it's not necessary (you can if you want).
mht-mustnt-dont-have-to.b0.1.1: *You **don't have to** tell me.* (You can if you want.)
mht-mustnt-dont-have-to.b1: ***Mustn't*** (*must not*) means you have an obligation **not** to do something: *You **mustn't** park here.*
mht-mustnt-dont-have-to.b2: ***Don't / doesn't have to*** means there is **no obligation**: *You **don't have to** pay. It's free.* You can do it, but it isn't necessary.
mht-mustnt-dont-have-to.b3: This is one of the most common mistakes. Ask yourself: *Is it forbidden?* → *mustn't*. *Is it optional?* → *don't have to*.
mht-must-vs-have-to.s: **must** often = the speaker thinks it's necessary. **have to** = a rule or situation makes it necessary. For the past and future, use **had to / will have to**.
mht-must-vs-have-to.b0.0.1: *I **have to** wear a uniform.* (the school decides)
mht-must-vs-have-to.b0.1.0: *You **must** come and see us.* (I want you to)
mht-must-vs-have-to.b0.1.1: *You **have to** show your passport.* (it's the law)
mht-must-vs-have-to.b1: In many sentences both are possible, especially in British English. But there's often a difference:
mht-must-vs-have-to.b2.0: ***must*** = the **speaker's** feeling or decision: *I **must** call her.* (I think it's important.)
mht-must-vs-have-to.b2.1: ***have to*** = an **outside** rule or situation: *I **have to** call her. It's my job.*
mht-must-vs-have-to.b3: In American English, *have to* (or *have got to*) is much more common than *must* for obligation.
mht-must-vs-have-to.b4: ***Have got to*** means the same as *have to*, and it's common in informal speech: *I**'ve got to** go.* It's only used in the present.
mht-past-future.t: Had to, will have to, have had to
mht-past-future.s: *Must* has no past or future form. Use **had to** for the past, **will have to** for the future, **have had to** for the present perfect.
mht-past-future.b1: Questions in the past: ***Did** you **have to** wait long?*
mht-past-future.b2: For the future, *must* and *have to* are possible when the decision is made now: *I **must / have to** leave early tomorrow.* Use ***will have to*** when the obligation will exist in the future: *If you fail, you**'ll have to** take the exam again.*
mht-need.t: Need to, don't need to, needn't
mht-need.s: **need to** = it's necessary. **don't need to / needn't** = it isn't necessary: *You **needn't** come. You **don't need to** come.*
mht-need.b0: ***Need to*** works like a normal verb: *I **need to** buy some milk. **Do** you **need to** leave?*
mht-need.b1: For **no necessity**, use ***don't need to*** or ***needn't*** (more British, a bit formal): *You **don't need to** shout. / You **needn't** shout.* Both mean the same as *don't have to*.
mht-need.b2: ***Needn't*** is followed by the base verb with no *to*: *You **needn't** worry.* Not *You needn't to worry*.
mht-need.b3: For the past, *didn't need to* and *needn't have* have different meanings. See [Should Have, Could Have, Needn't Have](/blog/grammar/should-have-could-have-neednt-have/).
x.mht-must-vs-have-to-s01: An outside authority (the doctor) decides: *have to*.
q.mht-must-vs-have-to-s02: Which sentence most clearly shows the speaker's own decision?
x.mht-must-vs-have-to-b03: *Have got to* is only for the present; for the past use *had to*.
q.mht-must-vs-have-to-b04: What's more common in American English?
x.mht-must-vs-have-to-b04: In AmE, *have to* is the usual choice.
x.mht-must-vs-have-to-b08: Past: *had to* (*must* has no past form).
x.mht-past-future-b03: *Might have to* = perhaps it will be necessary.
q.mht-need-b03: Which sentence has the same meaning as *You don't have to come*?
x.mht-need-b05: Not necessary: *don't need to buy* or *needn't buy*.
